title: Scale-dependent model-observation inconsistencies in global terrestrial water storage models
abstract: Accurate representation of terrestrial water storage is essential for water resource management and climate adaptation, yet model‑observation inconsistencies hinder global water cycle assessment. Here we show, using a unified multi‑scale framework, that seven model products with diverse modeling strategies and varying structural completeness exhibit scale‑dependent performance against Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment observations across global, climate-zone, and basin scales. Globally, hydrological models show the highest temporal correlation (0.94) but underperform spatially (0.32), whereas the assimilation system balances both dimensions with higher spatial agreement (0.73). Across climate zones, the assimilation system maintains robust performance, while physical models degrade in polar regions (−0.40). From large to small basin scales, hydrological model performance deteriorates systematically, whereas the assimilation system retains higher consistency and directional accuracy. These findings demonstrate that satellite observation-constrained assimilation substantially reduces inconsistencies relative to model‑driven products, offering essential guidance for climate adaptation and water management strategies. Using a satellite observation-constrained assimilation system can mitigate hydrological models’ inconsistencies, leading to improved global performance and maintaining robustness across various climate zones, according to analysis of model-observation inconsistencies across global, climate-zone, and multiple basin scales.
problem: Existing terrestrial water storage models exhibit scale-dependent inconsistencies with satellite observations, as models adequate at a global scale often fail at smaller watershed scales, hindering accurate water cycle assessment and local water resource management.
method: This study establishes a comprehensive multi-source, multi-scale evaluation framework to systematically assess seven terrestrial water storage modeling approaches against GRACE observations, revealing scale-dependent performance patterns and inconsistencies across global, climate-zone, and basin scales.
task: The task is to evaluate seven global terrestrial water storage model products against GRACE observations using a multi-scale framework to systematically assess their scale-dependent performance and inconsistencies across global, climate-zone, and basin scales.
innovation: Using a unified multi-scale framework, this paper systematically assesses seven global terrestrial water storage models against satellite observations, demonstrating that model-observation inconsistencies are scale-dependent and that data assimilation systems substantially reduce these discrepancies compared to physically-based models.

Nevertheless, in the products analyzed here, Noah v2.1 and VIC v2.1 do not explicitly represent deep groundwater storage, and in CLM 5.0 groundwater is represented by an unconfined aquifer scheme, which may still limit their ability to capture long-term water storage trends in regions dominated by deep aquifer dynamics and intensive groundwater abstraction.

ERA5-Land is a high-resolution global land surface reanalysis dataset that provides detailed information on terrestrial environmental changes12. Developed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), ERA5-Land is dynamically downscaled from ERA5 reanalysis outputs, which themselves assimilate a wide range of observations (e.g., temperature, relative humidity, and soil moisture) but do not assimilate GRACE observations60. It features high temporal resolution and a spatial resolution of 0.1° grid (approximately 9 km), covering the period from 1950 to the present, making it highly valuable in fields such as water cycle studies and climate change research.

To ensure direct comparability among all products, quantitative comparison based on Spearman rank correlation coefficient (CC) focused on the common overlapping period (2004.01–2014.12), which demonstrates marked performance disparities (Fig. 1b). All TWSA products maintain strong agreement with GRACE-derived TWSA observations (CC > 0.80), but CC values span from 0.80 to 0.94. WGHM achieves the highest agreement (CC = 0.94), whereas CLSM v2.2 exhibits comparatively lower correlation (CC = 0.80) despite its data assimilation framework.
Overall, the assimilation product CLSM v2.2 demonstrated high consistency across all five climate zones, with CC values ranging from 0.69 to 0.84, and NRMSE values ranging from 0.55 to 0.76.

Fig. 5 presents a comprehensive quantitative assessment of the NRE analysis results derived from four simulated TWSA products (Noah v2.1, CLSM v2.2, WGHM, ERA5-Land) and their mean values compared to GRACE observations. NRE is an information theory metric that has been widely employed to quantify the degree of difference between two spatial distributions, specifically in this context, lower NRE values indicate stronger congruence in spatial distribution between model simulations and GRACE observations, thereby signifying better product performance.

Notably, the CLSM v2.2 model best reproduces the observed correlation patterns from GRACE, especially within tropical and subtropical regions strongly influenced by ENSO, while other models exhibit varying degrees of bias in certain regions (e.g., the Amazon Basin and northern Australia), mainly due to insufficient simulation of hydrological extremes.

In contrast, other models showed commendable performance only in tropical and temperate climate zones, with CC values between 0.43 and 0.72. Their performance was notably lower in arid and cold climate zones (CC: 0.26 to 0.64), and even poorer in the polar climate zone (CC: -0.40 to 0.23), where some models, such as PCR-GLOBWB, exhibited opposite trends to GRACE observations.
